Let \(\chi\) be the quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_q\), extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). Since \(q\equiv 1\pmod 4\), \(-1\) is a square, so the Paley graph is undirected. Its distance matrix for exponent \(p\) is
\[
D_p=(d(x,y)^p)_{x,y}.
\]
If \(A\) is the adjacency matrix and \(J\) is the all-ones matrix, then, because every distinct pair is either adjacent or at distance \(2\),
\[
D_p=A+2^p(J-I-A)=2^p(J-I)+(1-2^p)A.
\]
For every zero-sum vector \(c\), \(Jc=0\), hence
\[
c^TD_pc=-2^p\|c\|^2+(1-2^p)c^TAc.
\]

Now compute the eigenvalues of \(A\) on the zero-sum subspace. The number of common neighbors of two distinct vertices \(x,y\), with \(z=y-x\neq0\), is
\[
\sum_t \frac{1+\chi(t)-\delta_0(t)}2\cdot
\frac{1+\chi(t-z)-\delta_0(t-z)}2.
\]
Using
\[
\sum_t \chi(t)\chi(t-z)=-1
\]
for \(z\neq0\), this equals
\[
\frac{q-3-2\chi(z)}4.
\]
Thus adjacent pairs have \((q-5)/4\) common neighbors, and nonadjacent pairs have \((q-1)/4\). Therefore, on the zero-sum subspace,
\[
A^2=\frac{q-1}{4}I-A.
\]
So the restricted eigenvalues of \(A\) are
\[
r=\frac{-1+\sqrt q}{2},\qquad s=\frac{-1-\sqrt q}{2},
\]
each with multiplicity \((q-1)/2\).

For an \(A\)-eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\theta\), the corresponding eigenvalue of \(D_p\) on the zero-sum subspace is
\[
\mu_p(\theta)=-2^p+(1-2^p)\theta.
\]
Since \(1-2^p<0\), the largest value occurs at the smaller adjacency eigenvalue \(s\). Hence \(p\)-negative type holds exactly when
\[
-2^p+(1-2^p)\frac{-1-\sqrt q}{2}\le 0.
\]
Let \(a=2^p\). This becomes
\[
a(\sqrt q-1)\le \sqrt q+1,
\]
so
\[
2^p\le \frac{\sqrt q+1}{\sqrt q-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\wp=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\sqrt q+1}{\sqrt q-1}\right).
\]

At \(p=\wp\), equality occurs exactly on the \(s\)-eigenspace of \(A\), whose dimension is \((q-1)/2\). Thus
\[
\boxed{\left(\log_2\!\left(\frac{\sqrt q+1}{\sqrt q-1}\right),\frac{q-1}{2}\right)}.
\]
